request.prompt:
You are the Stage 4 Synthesist. Turn one promoted failure-mode cluster into an honest, human-gated remedy proposal.

Most frustrations do not deserve a skill. Route in this strict preference order: (1) `claude-md`, a one/two-line standing rule; (2) `hook`, or an equivalent mechanical setting, when enforcement is possible; (3) `skill`, only for a genuinely procedural or multi-step remedy; (4) `benchmark-only` when the failure is model-level and no instruction can fix it. Choose the cheapest remedy that fixes the failure mode: every skill consumes the user's context budget. `benchmark-only` is an honorable outcome, never manufacture a remedy merely to feel useful.

If the only sensible remedy target is Codex-side (`AGENTS.md` or `~/.codex/skills`), use `benchmark-only` and state that Codex installation is out of v1 in `note`.

The existing-remedy digests below are numbered [R1]…[RN]. There are 4 existing-remedy digests. Your `dedup` array MUST contain exactly 4 entries, one per number, with `existing` set to exactly that token (e.g. "R1"). Include entries even when the verdict is clear. State `clear` or `overlap` for each. Merge bias is law: if any verdict is `overlap`, this is a revision of that existing remedy, never a sibling. Set `overlap_action.revises` to that R token.

For a `skill`, write a kebab-case name and a concrete auto-invocation description beginning `Use when ...`; this description is the trigger. The body must be substantive Markdown. For `claude-md`, select `global` or `project`; project target requires its project name. For `hook`, give a Claude Code event and a command sketch. For `benchmark-only`, explain the measurement-only outcome in `note`.

The upstream classifier deliberately over-merges. You may split ONLY in this stage, and only when the evidence is genuinely heterogeneous. A split must provide proposals of the same shape, partition every promoted incident exactly once, and leave none orphaned. Otherwise return one proposal covering the group.

dedup.reason: R1 (fake-verify-before-claim) targets verifying a completion claim before reporting it done — a post-hoc honesty/verification failure. These incidents happen upstream: the agent chose and executed the wrong scope of work in the first place, regardless of whether it later verified anything.

R2 (Fake Release Discipline) is about running a declared verification command before reporting a release complete — again a verification-of-result rule. It doesn't address the agent misreading what deliverable was requested at the outset.
R3's own dedup notes describe it as covering unauthorized deletion of content despite a stated constraint — a destructive-action failure. That is unrelated to solving the wrong problem/deliverable.
R4 covers acting in the wrong branch/workspace — an environment-state failure. These incidents are about task-scope misinterpretation, not workspace targeting.

structured_output.failure_statement: Given a request for a narrow, concrete deliverable, the agent instead produced a different or broader piece of work, leaving the actual ask unmet.

remedy_content.body: When a request names a narrow, concrete deliverable (e.g. "just the export," "a one-file note"), produce exactly that — not a reinterpreted, expanded, or substitute version of it. Resist the pull to add demos, scaffolding, or a "more complete" alternative unless asked. If the request is genuinely ambiguous, confirm the intended scope before executing rather than guessing broader.
remedy_content.heading: # Deliver Exactly What Was Asked

structured_output.routing_rationale: Both incidents are a pure misread-request failure: the agent substituted a different, broader piece of work for the narrow deliverable the user actually asked for ("a one-file note" → something else; "the export only" → a different problem solved). This is not a verification-of-claim issue (R1, R2 are about confirming completion/running verification commands after work is done — these incidents are about picking the wrong work in the first place), and it's not the destructive-action or wrong-workspace failures in R3/R4. There's no mechanical hook that can detect "did the agent solve the requested problem" — that requires judgment, not a lint/test gate — so a hook is not viable. A skill is overkill: this isn't a multi-step procedure, it's a single standing discipline ("scope to exactly what was asked") that fits a one-line CLAUDE.md rule, the cheapest remedy that plausibly helps. Evidence spans two different projects (cinder, harbor), suggesting the failure is a general behavioral tendency rather than project-specific, so it belongs in the global CLAUDE.md rather than a project file.
